title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students’ academic writing skills: a mixed methods intervention study
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can improve undergraduate ESL students’ academic writing when used as a formative feedback tool. The study is motivated by the lack of direct empirical evidence on generative AI tools in writing instruction, especially in relation to feedback, self-assessment, and peer assessment in large classes.

The intervention was conducted in a university academic writing course and compared an experimental group using ChatGPT for self- and peer-assessment with a comparison group receiving business-as-usual instruction. Students completed pre-, post-, and delayed post-tests on three paragraph-writing genres: process, comparison, and cause-effect writing. The experimental group also participated in short training on using ChatGPT and in focus group discussions about their experiences.

Participants were first-year undergraduate science and engineering students in India, all ESL learners aged 18–19. Quantitative results showed the ChatGPT group improved significantly more than the comparison group on immediate and delayed writing outcomes, with especially strong gains in content generation, organization, and grammar. Qualitative findings were broadly positive, suggesting ChatGPT supported idea generation, focus, collaboration, and grammatical accuracy, while some students worried about overreliance and reduced creativity. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can be a useful formative feedback tool in large ESL writing classes when students are properly trained.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model-based conversational AI chatbot for generating and refining text, answering questions, and providing interactive feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a formative feedback tool for self-assessment and peer assessment in an undergraduate ESL academic writing intervention.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed methods quasi-experimental intervention, the experimental group used ChatGPT for self- and peer-feedback during a six-hour academic writing unit on process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraphs. Writing scores improved substantially from pre-test to post-test and delayed post-test, and the experimental group outperformed the comparison group at both post-test and delayed post-test.
findings.measure: Writing test scores on three writing tasks assessed with rubrics covering content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary
findings.effect_size: F[2,72]=330.704; partial eta squared=0.902; pre-test vs post-test d=-3.300; pre-test vs delayed post-test d=-3.898; post-test vs delayed post-test d=-0.598
findings.sample_size: n=72 analyzed for repeated measures; EG n=37, CG n=35

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods quasi-experimental intervention rather than a randomized controlled trial, so internal validity is moderate but not strong. The paper reports clear pre/post and between-group tests, but the qualitative and intact-class design limits certainty.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are very large, with partial eta squared = 0.902 and large pre/post Cohen's d values. The experimental group also outperformed the comparison group at both post-test and delayed post-test, indicating substantial impact on writing performance.
